Vignette: Wiremu, Age 71

Wiremu grew up on the North Island of New Zealand, the son of a Māori fisherman, and spent most of his adult life building a quiet reputation as a landscape painter. His canvases were known for their stillness - wide harbours at dusk, hills folded into mist, the kind of light that asks nothing of you. He traveled occasionally to sell his work at exhibitions, and it was one of those trips, seven years ago, that changed everything.

He was in a crowded marketplace in a city he had always wanted to visit when the explosion happened. He does not talk about the details easily, and when he does, the words come out in fragments - the sound first, then the pressure against his chest, then the silence that followed, which he describes as the worst part. He was not physically wounded, though the man standing two metres to his left was killed. Wiremu helped carry a young woman to the roadside before emergency services arrived. He does not know whether she survived.

He flew home three days later and told almost no one what had happened. He went back to his studio, picked up his brushes, and tried to return to the life he had before. For a few weeks, it almost worked.

Then the dreams began. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, certain he can smell smoke even though there is none. He lies in the dark of his small house outside Tauranga and waits for his body to believe it is safe. Sometimes it takes hours. He lives alone - a long relationship ended in his fifties, and he has not sought another - and the nights feel very long now.

During the day, he avoids the news entirely. He stopped going to the Saturday market in town about a year after returning home, and he has not been able to explain to his daughter, who lives in Auckland, exactly why he cancelled his last two visits to the city. Crowded places make him feel as though the ground beneath him is unreliable. He scans exits when he enters a room. He keeps his back to walls in the rare instances he does go out for coffee or groceries.

His painting has changed in ways that trouble him. He used to work in broad, unhurried strokes, but now he finds himself unable to sustain attention on a canvas for more than twenty or thirty minutes before something - a car backfiring outside, a shadow moving across the window - pulls him out of the work entirely. He describes it as being unable to fully enter the painting the way he once could. Several canvases sit unfinished against the studio wall. He looks at them and feels a grief he cannot quite name.

He is irritable in ways that are foreign to his own sense of himself. He snapped at his nephew last Christmas and spent the following week ashamed of it. He describes himself as having become "a smaller person" - less generous, less patient, less present. He used to find the act of painting meditative, a way of settling into the world. Now the studio is a place where he goes and tries, and often fails.

What keeps him going, he says, is the work itself - or the memory of what the work once felt like. He still believes he has paintings left in him. He still rises early and walks down to the water before breakfast, watching the light move across the harbour the way it always has. But he watches it now from a careful distance, as though beauty has become something that requires a certain vigilance, as though peace is a thing that can be taken without warning, and he has learned, at seventy-one, that this is simply true.
